newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA DENIES WRONGDOING IN MIAMI ARMS CASE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA DENIES WRONGDOING IN MIAMI ARMS CASE.

text.p: Bulgaria's trade ministry has denied any wrongdoing in the case of two Lithuanians arrested in the United States for trying to sell Bulgarian-made weapons to U.S. undercover agents posing as Colombian drug dealers.

A ministry statement published by Bulgarian newspapers on Wednesday said a legal licence was issued on December 16, 1996 for Bulgarian state company Armimex to export weapons to U.S. firm Phoenix Arms International for final delivery to the Lithuanian defence ministry.
It said the deal was not completed because the buyer was unable to pay.

"The American company has an exclusive representative, Alexander Darichev, a Lithuanian citizen, who misused his powers and led negotiations on that deal in violation of the sealed export documents," the statement said.
"The Bulgarian side does not bear responsibility in this case."

Darichev and Alexander Progrebeshski pleaded not guilty in Miami on Monday on charges of conspiring to ship explosive materials and missiles without a licence and conspiring to transfer nuclear materials unlawfully.
Both were ordered jailed without bond.
They had offered to supply the undercover agents with shoulder-fired, portable, surface-to-air missiles known as the SAM-14 (Strela) and SAM-16 (Igla).

The owner of a cargo ship registered in Equatorial Guinea offered to ship the weapons from Bourgas, Bulgaria, to Puerto Rico in a load of junk materials that would pass inspection at the Straits of Gibraltar, the arrest affidavit said.
Bulgaria's once-flourishing arms industry producing Soviet weapons has declined since the end of communist rule in 1989 but Bulgarian-made weapons are still in demand in conflict areas.
